claims.text: The initial single-crystal FeNiCrMn alloy has an FCC crystal structure.
The initial crystal is free of pre-existing dislocations and phase boundaries.
The crystal orientation should maximize resolved shear stress on the primary slip system.
Atomic-size mismatch among the constituent elements produces severe local lattice distortion.
Local lattice distortion creates a fluctuating potential-energy landscape that impedes dislocation motion.
Yielding is dominated by thermally activated dislocation nucleation and glide.
Severe local lattice distortion produces a high lattice-friction or Peierls barrier.
FCC-to-BCC phase transformation is not the dominant process at yield.
Simple dislocation multiplication is not the dominant process at yield.
Yield-initiating dislocations nucleate from the crystal surface or specific defects.
The yield-controlling process has a large activation volume.
A large activation volume makes the nucleation stress weakly dependent on strain rate.
Yield strength decreases strongly as temperature increases from 77 K to 600 K.
Yield strength remains relatively insensitive to strain rate between 10^-4 s^-1 and 10^2 s^-1.
Traditional FCC metals exhibit a strong positive correlation between yield strength and strain rate.
Dislocation multiplication causes the stronger strain-rate dependence attributed to traditional FCC metals.
Grain-boundary sliding or twinning may dominate deformation in polycrystalline variants.
Alloys containing significant BCC phase fractions operate through different deformation mechanisms.
Observation of a significant BCC population at the onset of yield would falsify the proposed non-transformation mechanism.
A strain-rate sensitivity exponent greater than 0.05 would indicate that phase transformation or dislocation multiplication is dominant.

contradictions.description: The material and applicability boundary define a quaternary FeNiCrMn alloy, but the mediator invokes Co 'if present,' implicitly broadening the mechanism to a five-component CoCrFeMnNi system without defining a corresponding change in composition or scope.
